title: Batch heating and cooling
ends: Your batches will hit temperature on time.

steps.q: How much heat does it take to warm 5000 kg of batch (Cp 0.5 kcal/kg °C) from 25 to 75 °C?
board: How much heat does it take
steps.title: Heat needed
steps.summary: Heat required is mass × heat capacity × temperature rise: 5000 kg × 0.5 kcal/kg °C × 50 °C = 125,000 kcal, plus some heat for the vessel steel. How long it takes depends on the jacket's heat transfer.

draw: how long? → depends on the jacket

steps.q: A batch heats quickly at first, then slows down near the jacket temperature. Why?
steps.title: Shrinking ΔT
steps.summary: Heat flow is U × A × (jacket temperature − batch temperature). As the batch warms, the temperature difference shrinks, so heat flow falls and the batch approaches the jacket temperature ever more slowly. The last few degrees always take the longest.

draw: Q = U × A × (T jacket − T batch)

steps.q: Jacket 120 °C, batch 25 → 75 °C, mCp 2500 kcal/°C, UA 2500 kcal/h °C. How long?
steps.title: Heat-up time
steps.summary: With a jacket at constant temperature, heat-up time t = (mCp ÷ UA) × ln[(Tj − T1) ÷ (Tj − T2)]. Here mCp ÷ UA = 2500 ÷ 2500 = 1 h and ln(95 ÷ 45) ≈ 0.75, so t ≈ 0.75 h, about 45 minutes. Heating on from 75 to 115 °C takes ln(45 ÷ 5) ≈ 2.2 h, three times longer for fewer degrees.

steps.q: The same batch, in a taller reactor, covers only half the jacket. Heat-up time?
steps.title: Wetted area
steps.summary: Only the vessel wall in contact with the batch transfers heat, so the same batch in a taller vessel, covering only part of the jacket, heats more slowly. A hot jacket above the liquid can also bake product onto the dry wall. Use the heat transfer area at the actual level, heat only the zones below it where possible, and make sure the temperature probe and agitator are submerged.

steps.q: A glass-lined reactor cools slowly, even with brine. What usually limits it?
steps.title: Glass limits U
steps.summary: Heat crosses the batch-side film, the glass lining, the steel wall and the jacket-side film. Glass conducts heat roughly forty times worse than steel, so even a thin lining is a large resistance and glass-lined reactors have a much lower overall coefficient U than steel vessels, often a few hundred kcal/h m² °C. Faster agitation helps only a little; plan for longer cooling times.

draw: U lower than a steel vessel

steps.q: A glass-lined reactor is at 150 °C. Why not send cold brine straight into the jacket?
steps.title: Thermal shock
steps.summary: Glass and steel expand differently, so a sudden temperature change on either side stresses the lining and can crack or spall the glass, taking the vessel out of service. Every glass-lined vessel has a thermal shock chart from its manufacturer; stay within it and cool in stages, for example hot water, then cooling water, then brine, draining the jacket between each.

opts.t: Thermal shock can crack the glass

draw: too big a jump → cracked glass
stage it: hot water → CW → brine

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: heating and cooling a batch in a jacketed reactor. Why it always takes longer than you think. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Now work out your own heat-up time in the jacketed vessel calculator.

q1.text: Question 1. How much heat does it take to warm 5000 kg of batch (Cp 0.5 kcal/kg °C) from 25 to 75 °C?

q1-r1.text: You forgot the 0.5. That's water's heat capacity, not this batch's.

q1-r2.text: A zero went missing somewhere. Check again.

q1-b0.text: Heat equals mass times heat capacity times the temperature rise.

q1-b2.text: That's 125,000 kilocalories, plus the vessel steel, often a sizeable extra.

q1-b3.text: The heat is the easy part. How long it takes depends on the jacket, as the next questions show.

q2.text: Question 2. A batch heats quickly at first, then slows down near the jacket temperature. Why?

q2-r0.text: The steam is still there. It just has less to push against.

q2-r1.text: Yes! Less difference, less heat flow.

q2-r2.text: The agitator runs at the same speed. Look at the driving force.

q2-r3.text: Possibly, but even water does this. It's the driving force.

q2-b0.text: Heat flow is U times A times the difference between jacket and batch.

q2-b1.text: As the batch warms, that difference shrinks. So the heat flow falls.

q2-b2.text: The batch creeps towards the jacket temperature but never quite gets there.

q2-b3.text: So the last few degrees are always the slowest.

q3.text: Question 3. Jacket 120 °C, batch 25 → 75 °C, mCp 2500 kcal/°C, UA 2500 kcal/h °C. How long?

q3-r0.text: Too quick. The shrinking temperature difference slows it.

q3-r1.text: Too slow for this step. Check the log term.

q3-r2.text: That's closer to heating on to 115. Not this step.

q3-b0.text: For a jacket at constant temperature, time equals m C p over U A, times a log term.

q3-b1.text: m C p over U A is 2500 over 2500: one hour. The log term is the log of 95 over 45, which is about 0.75.

q3-b3.text: Going on from 75 to 115 takes the log of 45 over 5, about 2.2 hours. Three times longer for fewer degrees.

q4.text: Question 4. The same batch, in a taller reactor, covers only half the jacket. Heat-up time?

q4-r0.text: Same batch, but only the wetted wall works. Less area, slower.

q4-r1.text: Yes! Only the wall touching liquid counts.

q4-r2.text: A bigger vessel doesn't help if the batch only wets half of it.

q4-r3.text: The jacket doesn't care about the batch level.

q4-b0.text: Only the wall in contact with the batch transfers heat into it.

q4-b1.text: Same mass, less area. m C p over U A goes up, so it takes longer.

q4-b2.text: A hot jacket above the liquid can bake product onto the dry wall. Check the temperature probe and the agitator blades are under the liquid too.

q4-b3.text: Use the area at your actual level, and heat only the jacket zones below it if you can.

q5.text: Question 5. A glass-lined reactor cools slowly, even with brine. What usually limits it?

q5-r0.text: The glass! Great for corrosion, poor for heat.

q5-r1.text: Steel conducts heat well. It's not the bottleneck.

q5-r2.text: Colder brine helps. It's not the limit.

q5-r3.text: Volume sets how much heat, not how fast it moves.

q5-b0.text: Heat crosses the batch film, the glass, the steel, and the jacket film.

q5-b1.text: Glass conducts heat about forty times worse than carbon steel. A thin layer is still a big resistance.

q5-b2.text: So glass-lined reactors have a much lower U than steel ones, often a few hundred kilocalories per square metre per hour per degree.

q5-b3.text: Faster agitation helps only a little. Plan for the longer cooling time.

q6.text: Question 6. A glass-lined reactor is at 150 °C. Why not send cold brine straight into the jacket?

q6-r0.text: It won't freeze against a 150 degree wall. The glass is the problem.

q6-r1.text: Yes! Glass hates sudden temperature changes.

q6-r2.text: The pump's fine. The glass is not.

q6-r3.text: It does, but that's the least of your worries.

q6-b0.text: Glass and steel expand differently. A sudden temperature jump stresses the glass.

q6-b1.text: Too big a jump, hot side or cold side, and the glass can crack or spall. Then the vessel is out of service.

q6-b2.text: Every glass-lined vessel has a thermal shock chart from its maker. Stay inside it.

q6-b3.text: Cool in stages: hot water, then cooling water, then brine, draining the jacket between each. Check your timings in the jacketed vessel calculator on pharmacheme dot in.
